# Download the data {#sec-download-data}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| eval: true
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(downlit)
```

You'll be using a synthetic dataset (generated from real data) during the
code-along portion of the workshop. This dataset is an openly licensed dataset
from Zenodo with data on basic clinical characteristics and disease
status\ [@CSD2026]. You can check out this [dataset on
Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/22996512) for more details about it.

Unlike the [intermediate workshop](https://r-cubed-intermediate.rostools.org),
we will not be doing any processing or cleaning of the research data. We'll
provide a relatively clean and tidy dataset for you to use during this workshop.
If you want to see what we did to tidy it up, check out the [R script on the
GitHub
repo](https://github.com/rostools/r-cubed-advanced/blob/main/data-raw/cv-risk.R).
However, just like in the intermediate workshop, you'll still create a script in
`data-raw/` that will download the dataset and save it to the `data/` folder.

First step, you'll create this R script by typing and running the following code
in the R Console pane while in your `AdvancedR3` R Project:

```{r}
#| label: create-data-raw
#| filename: Console
#| purl: true
#| eval: false

usethis::use_data_raw("cv-risk")
```

This function creates a new folder called `data-raw/` in your project (if it
didn't exist already) and creates an R script called `cv-risk.R` in that folder.
The R script should have opened up for you, otherwise, go into the `data-raw/`
folder and open up the new `nmr-omics.R` script. The first thing to do is
**delete all the code in the script**. Than, copy and paste the code below into
the script. You can run the lines one at a time and see what they do on your own
or `source()` the file all at once. The comments provided give guidance on what
the code is doing and why.

```{r}
#| label: download-cv-risk-data
#| eval: false
#| purl: true

cv_risk_path <- here::here("data", "cv-risk.csv")
if (!fs::file_exists(cv_risk_path)) {
  download.file(
    "https://r-cubed-advanced.rostools.org/data/cv-risk.csv",
    destfile = cv_risk_path,
    # For in Windows users.
    mode = "wb"
  )
}
```

After running this code (either line-by-line or via `source()`), you should now
have the `cv-risk.csv` dataset saved in the `data/cv-risk.csv` file. The created
files should look like this:

```{r}
#| label: admin-print-data-raw-tree
#| echo: false
#| eval: false

fs::dir_tree(regexp = "data(-raw)?")
```

```text
AdvancedR3
├── data
│   └── cv-risk.csv
└── data-raw
    └── cv-risk.R
```

::: callout-tip
The created dataset in `data/cv-risk.csv` should look like the below when
loading it using `readr::read_csv()`. You don't need to run this code, this is
only to show you what the data looks like.

```{r}
#| label: read-cv-risk
#| eval: true

readr::read_csv(here::here("data/cv-risk.csv"))
```

Take a look through the [dataset's Zenodo
page](https://zenodo.org/records/22996512) if you'd like to learn more about the
data, though this isn't required as we will go through it during the workshop.
:::

You'll be using Git to track changes made to files in our project. For a normal
data analysis project that is tracked by Git, you shouldn't commit data files.
That's because Git:

- Isn't really designed to handle large data.
- If you are analyzing personal and sensitive data, you don't want to store that
  data in your Git history as it will make it harder to share your code and Git
  repository with others.

```{r}
#| label: purl-store-data
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
#| purl: true

git_ci(
  c("data-raw/cv-risk.R", "data/cv-risk.csv"),
  "Download data into data folder"
)
```

need to paste this output into the survey at the end.

```r {filename="Console"}
r3::check_project_setup_advanced()
```

If you encounter an error that says something like "Error in `gh::gh()`", you
can (potentially) solve it by running `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()` in the Console
as you did in @sec-setup-github and then running the
`r3::check_project_setup_advanced()` command again.
:::

The output should look something a bit like the above text. If it doesn't, start
over by deleting everything in the `data-raw/` folder *except* for the
`data-raw/cv-risk.R` script and re-running the script again. If your output
looks a bit like the above, than copy and paste the output into the survey
question at the end.

## Automatically adhere to a style guide

We've covered how to adhere to a style guide in both the introductory and
intermediate workshop, because it is such a useful and powerful tool to easily
write more readable code. We'll expand on it in this workshop because it fits
precisely with the theme of collaboration. That's because, when you're working
on your own and don't need to worry about anyone seeing your code, there's a
natural temptation to write your code like you might write notes to yourself:
scribbled and scrawled down quickly.

But when working with others, how it looks can greatly impact how quickly and
easily others are able to read and interpret your code. Multiply all the
collaborators on a project with this natural temptation for quick (and
potentially sloppy) coding, you can imagine how easy it is for code to massively
"drift" towards being poorly formatted, especially when deadlines are
approaching.

That's when "linters" or "stylers" (types of static code analysis tools) become
very useful. They scan your code for common mistakes or syntax issues, either
listing them for you to fix or automatically fixing them for you. Linters are
especially useful in ensuring the code is consistently formatted across the
project when collaborating with someone who is less experienced with coding or
who contributes occasionally.

To ensure consistent styling without needing to run checks manually, *automatic*
linting/styling can be a great solution. That's where the `{styler}` package
comes in!

There are only a few functions in `{styler}` that we can to use. The first is
used to style a single file with R code in it using `styler::style_file()`.
However, an easier way to style the file we're currently working on is the
"style active file" RStudio addin. We use that through the Command Palette
({{< var keybind.palette >}}) and typing "style file", which should show the
"Style active file" option. This is what we will do frequently throughout the
workshop.

Let's try it out. While inside the `data-raw/cv-risk.R` file, use
{{< var keybind.styler >}} to style the file. Notice that no changes were made
since the file is already formatted.

::: {.callout-note appearance="default"}
You will probably be asked to install a package called `{miniUI}`, click "Yes".
:::

If you wanted to run `{styler}` on all the files, you can use:

```{r}
#| label: style-dir
#| eval: false
#| filename: Console

styler::style_dir()
```

Now that you are done, you can commit the changes by either using the Git
interface or by running the below functions in the Console.

With the Git interface, open it with either the Git icon at the top near the
menu bar or with {{< var keybind.git >}}. While in the interface, select all the
current changes by clicking the checkbox beside the files and stage them. Then
write a commit message in the text box on the right, something like
`Download and save data`. Click the "Commit" button, and finally close the Git
interface.

**If you have never used the Git interface before**, you can instead copy and
paste these R functions to do the same thing. So paste these functions into the
Console and run them:

```{r}
#| label: add-data-to-git-history
#| filename: "Console"
#| eval: false

gert::git_add(".")
gert::git_commit("Download and save data")
```
